# Executive Summary
AI is being rolled out to every process, workflow, activity in both the business and personal domains. Office workers send AI-generated emails to each other, ask AI for advice, technical and personal, generate content for others to consume, who likely use AI to further summarize. 

In some of these use cases, AI use is warranted and even encouraged. In others, AI output requires human review. And in some of the cases, AI use should be largely avoided.

In this article I introduce a rough 3-layered mental model for categorizing areas of AI use, human oversight, and where the frontier AI-capabilities currently overlap with human intelligence.

# Part 1 - How we think and communicate 
Consider a case, where I need a particular recipe for a carrot cake. I'm no baker, and have no recipes in mind, so I decide to ask AI to generate one for me. I receive a generated recipe back: 

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

I**

I immediately ask myself 3 questions:

- Does this look like a correct recipe? -> Yes - with a quick glance, this has the characteristics of a carrot cake recipe
- Is this a correct recipe? Perhaps - the ingredients look right, but I'm no baker, so I don't know if that's too much sugar, or if the ratios here are correct. Don't there need to be eggs?
- Is this the most correct recipe out of the possible set of correct recipes? I don't know - I'm sure there are different ways to make good carrot cakes. I'm not sure what those are, what variables of the recipe a baker might change. Is sweeter batter better or perhaps sweeter frosting? And therefore I cannot determine where this recipe sits on this scale.
  

Simply, I'm trying to determine 3 things, in this order:
- This **looks** like the correct solution
- This **is a** correct solution
- This **is the** correct solution out of a set of several possible correct solutions 

This, in essence, is the 3 layered verification process our mind goes through. This triplet set of questioning happens almost unconsciously, in many scenarios in our lives, and has been around long before AI: 


  

- When you receive a bill, you glance at it quickly - does it look correct? - is it calculated correctly? - is it the exact correct calculation given everything I know about this bill. 
    

- When someone walks up to you on the street, you immediately attempt to  judge first impressions, listen to what they say, attempt to understand who they are. Do they look trustworthy? Is this person trustworthy based on what they are saying and doing? Is this the behaviour I would expect from a person in this scenario on the street? 
    
- When picking a piece of fruit at a market. You're not quite sure if it's fresh or about to go off. With a quick visual inspection, you determine, does it look ok? It seems fine. You perform more checks, give it a squeeze, a quick smell, is it fresh? Everything seems fine. Your final thought - from what I know about the best watermelons I've ever had, is this the kind of colour, size, sound, smell and feeling I would expect?
    
- When you attend a talk, lecture, or are just listening to someone speak, your first filter is, are they articulate? Does their use of language appear / look to be well constructed? If it is, then does what they are saying make sense (is it correct)? And finally, if it does, is it the most valid perspective or correct point on the topic they're referring to? 
    

  

This verification triplet is a heuristic we use, to navigate the world efficiently and safely. It allows us to establish a tradeoff between safety and speed. If I'm reading an article riddled with spelling and grammar mistakes, I will already begin to infer that the content of what is being said is likely incorrect, due to the relationship between form and content. The likelihood that someone who hasn't made the effort to proof read their article or is unable to construct coherent sentences, has also not put in the same effort into the though and concepts of what they are saying, is high. The opposite is true, if I begin to read an article or book that is incredibly worded and articulate, I will begin to infer that there probably is something worthy in the content of what is being said - simply by inferring from the form of the text (grammar, spelling, syntax). 

  

This heuristic allows me to filter out 80% of the likely less desirable articles, and saves me time from reading them. It is however not 100% effective as it may inadvertently penalise a small percentage who struggle with articulation and form, who nonetheless have a very good point to make. That is why this is a heuristic, or a shortcut. 

  

This can be applied to all other situations above, if someone walks up to me on the street, rough fair, ripped, stained clothes, looking dishevelled, my guard goes up and I set my trust levels low. I may be wrong! They may just be having a bad day. But there's a high probability that there's something going on here, and in the game of life and probabilities, we plan for the most likely outcome.

  

So what does this have to do with AI?

  

AI has conquered Layer 1, is exceedingly good at Layer 2 with human guidance, whilst Layer 3 remains out of reach and largely still a human intelligence domain.

  

# Part 2 - 3 Layers of information communication 

Producers and Consumers

In all forms of information communication, there is a producer and a consumer. In a conversation where I am currently the active speaker, I am currently the producer, producing sounds through my mouth that translate to words that relate to ideas and concepts that I want to convey to the listeners, who are the consumers of my speech.

  

The 3 layers of information communication look something like this.

  

![](data:image/png;base64,)

  

|   |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|
|Layer|Name|Description|Examples|
|Layer 1|Form|The appearance, presentation, and style. The 'wrapping' of the content into a form. This is the first thing to be perceived|Language,  audio, image, video|
|Layer 2|Content|The message, idea, concept, 'thing' that is packaged in the form. The same content can typically be expressed in various forms.|A recipe, an idea or thought,|
|Layer 3|Context|The 'global' context of similar or relating content. Information that is not strictly part of the content, but could be, and is somehow related.|All recipes|

  

## The typical flow of information between producer and consumer - why these layers function 

As a producer of communication, my information flows bottom up.

  

Layer 3: The producer starts by considering the whole global concept of a topic or question. If someone asks me "what is the best way to bake a cake" or "what's a quick way to drive through the city?" or "how can we help grow the company" or "how can I improve my health?" or "why is my server down". Thought almost always begins from layer 3, especially when multiple correct answers exist, with various assumptions and consequences to each. I formulate a hypothesis and select a few paths.

One might refer to this as a 'fan-out' approach - considering multiple angles of a problem, taking different perspectives. I've considered a few recipes that fit the requirements.

  

Layer 2:  Once I'm satisfied with my consideration of the global context, making sure I've taken everything into account, I settle on a few correct answers (or one) and eventually make a decision to present a response. In layer two, I begin to articulate why this response is the correct path. Because I've already done my reasoning through Layer 3, I am easily able to articulate why my chosen approach is not only correct, but is the correct approach when considered against others. The aspects of the approach that make it unique are the reasons it was chosen and I am able to articulate the advantages. I now have a clear message that I want to communicate. 

  

Layer 1: The packaging of the message. Whether as text, as a diagram, as a video, communicated in speech or some other medium. I now need to find the right words, images etc. that properly articulate what I am trying to say about the approach I have settled on. 

  

This leads us to the first intuition

"intuition 1 - For producers, clarity of thought is a precursor for clarity of communication. The reverse becomes true for consumers. When a form of communication appears articulate, clear, structured, the more the consumer assumes that the message  and underlying content is well thought through and clear." 

  

If a producer has experience in a field (layer 3), which allows them to provide correct answers to questions (layer 2), in a clearly articulated manner (layer 1) then this generates confidence in the consumers that the reverse sequence can be used as a heuristic for quality and trustworthiness of producers. 

  

i.e. if the form (layer 1) is well presented, then the content and message is likely well constructed and reasoned (layer 2) and if that is well reasoned and constructed, it follows that it was done so with knowledge of a global context of other correct similar paths.

  

As humans, likely over long periods of time, we have evolved to use layer 1, the form layer, to make judgments on things and move through the world that way.

# Part 3 - What this means for AI use

## 'Form' is now a false friend - AI has conquered layer 1, through mastery of mimicry 

Generative AI models have now become so good that it is increasingly more difficult for humans to tell whether a piece of content was generated by an AI or a human

  

### Humans fight back: "Did you send me something AI Generated" ? 

As AIs improve and evolve, humans are also not standing still. We continue to leverage our layer 1 heuristic as a filter to navigate the world. 

  

There is a growing trend of people refusing to read content sent to them by colleagues where they believe the content was AI generated. "AI Slop" and "AI Smells" are becoming common. 

  

The heuristic is - if the layer 1 form appears to be AI generated, then I can infer that layer 2 - the content - may not be entirely correct and almost definitely layer 3 - is absent (the absence of knowing if this is the best solution). 

  

Evidence of AI generation in Layer 1 has become a proxy for potential loss of quality at Layer 2 and lack of quality at Layer 3. Put simply, if you send me an AI generated 10-page strategy document or technical software document, I am going to assume that the content (layer 2) is likely not entirely correct and that there may be other global considerations (layer 3) that are valid that were completely missed. 

  

## What this means for the future of work

Tasks where the value is in Layer 1 -> can safely be handed over to AI:

- Generating and sending a nicely worded message
    
- Summarizing notes of a meeting
    
- Explaining the content of a code repository
    
- Search
    

  

Tasks where the value is in Layer 2 -> these can be generated with AI but require human review:

- Designing a code solution 
    
- Formulating a plan or strategy
    

  

Tasks where the value is in Layer 3 -> these almost definitely need to be at least human led. If any AI generation is used, these must be grounded in verbose human provided instructions and guardrails on policies, how to conduct reasoning over the problem space and any and all constraints, assumptions and perspectives that might naturally be considered by a highly experienced SME:

- RCA or cause and effect analysis
    
- Long-horizon strategic decisions in complex systems (economic decisions) 
    
- etc.
